prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I keep B006 as my single-part configuration and I have not changed it since round 1; what has changed is the wording and my confidence in the reasoning. Having read the full exchange and the chair's questions, the case rests on three scientific points and not on the count of supporters. First, the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct physical idea: it removes the old trade-off between the number of interrogated atoms, which sets stability, and the perturbation of the clock transition, which sets accuracy. That is not a refinement of the frequency comb (2005), which is a ruler for optical frequencies, nor of Wineland's single-ion work (2012), which uses one trapped ion and a different systematic budget. Second, the result is the kind I trust as an instrument builder: quantified, with systematics traced to physical causes, and reproduced at RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB and SYRTE, and surpassed by independent groups. Third, it has already given measurements nobody could do before, such as the gravitational redshift across a millimetre-sized sample, and it is the route to the redefinition of the second and to sensitive searches for varying constants and dark matter. The credit is a lineage of idea (Katori) and realisation at record performance (Ye) and fits the three-person limit without a visible gap.
statement.case_against: The overlap objection with 2005 and 2012 is not fully answered; it is answered only if the citation names the invention and its realisation and not a precision record. The attribution objection is real: Ludlow, Lemonde, Hinkley, Bloom and the Yb, Hg, Al+ and ion-clock communities contributed to the 10^-18 milestone, and I know the 2001-03 priority record only from memory. If an expert report showed that the magic-wavelength priority were genuinely shared, or that the record-performance credit belonged more broadly than to Ye, I would reopen the credit and might consider a third name. The redefinition of the second has not happened, so the largest practical payoff is still ahead, which cuts both ways on timing.

responses.point: Bernhard Mehlig prefers B009, magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, for its mechanism-first logic: a compact Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 experimental discovery, with B004 as the more settled alternative.
responses.response: I accept that the prediction-to-discovery link is the cleanest in condensed matter on our list, and that the phenomena have been reproduced widely; I am not dismissing the science. Two things stop me from moving to B009. The pairing mechanism for the superconductivity is unresolved, and the field is about eight years old, so I cannot tell what the lasting result will be: the tunable flat-band platform, or particular phases that may be reinterpreted. You also concede yourself that the experimental credit is awkward, since Yuan Cao and other first authors are outside a three-name limit that you want to spend partly on Bistritzer. A clock result is the opposite case, where the mechanism is understood and the numbers have been checked by competing groups. I keep B009 as an alternative and would reconsider it in a few years.

responses.point: Olle Eriksson prefers B004, topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect, as a new symmetry-protected state of matter with a decisive HgTe experiment and almost twenty years of independent confirmation, and asks whether a new state of matter should take priority over a better ruler.
responses.response: That question is fair, and I am an experimentalist who values new states of matter. My answer is that the prize has also gone to new ways of measuring, when the measurement opens a window that was closed, and the clock does that. On B004 I am not the right person to judge the Z2 step against the 2016 prize, and I note that you accept the credit boundary is untidy: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route that Molenkamp realised, and the three-dimensional phase belongs to Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents and Hasan. A three-name award has to leave out someone whose contribution was decisive. If you can state which of those omissions the committee could defend, and why the overlap with 2016 is not repetition, I would put B004 above B009 as my first alternative; I have ranked it that way.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth keeps B006 first, argues that the prize rewards an idea and its realisation, and admits she has not settled how to weigh Katori's concept against the performance records from Ye's group.
responses.response: I share that open point and think the committee should treat it as the main task before voting, not as a footnote. My view is that the citation should be built on the concept and on the realisation, with the performance level as evidence, not as the achievement itself, which is the wording I propose. That wording gives Katori the idea and the first strontium lattice clocks, and Ye the demonstration that the idea scales to a many-body clock with the best systematics. I do not think we should hide the weighing: if an expert report shows that Ye's group contributed more to the idea than I remember, the two-name pair becomes stronger; if it shows others hold a real part of the priority, the pair becomes harder to defend.

responses.point: Stefan Kroll discloses a year in John Hall's JILA laboratory during his PhD, reports no collaboration with Katori or Ye, and defers to the committee on recusal for B006.
responses.response: I do not think that disclosure is a reason to recuse. A doctoral year in the same environment as one candidate, with no joint work, is the sort of link that all of us have somewhere in this field, and it is better that you state it. I would ask the committee to note it in the record and let Kroll vote, with the proviso that I would weigh his view on Ye's priority with the same care as any other member's, and I would ask for the expert report on 2001-03 priority to come from outside the JILA and RIKEN circles. As Chair I will put the recusal question formally to the committee so that Kroll, Lindroth and Johansson are handled in the same way.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as a new invention rather than a precision advance after the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes; I think it is, but this rests on a judgement about concept and not on a measured fact.

Priority in the magic-wavelength proposal and in the 10^-18 milestone among Katori, Ye and the Ludlow, Lemonde, Hinkley, NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups, which I know from memory and which needs an independent expert report before the credit is final.

Whether a second distinct part could be added without exceeding three laureates; I see no candidate on the shortlist that would improve the configuration, since B004, B009 and B043 each have an unresolved credit or maturity issue of their own.
Whether B004 is distinct enough from the 2016 topological-phases prize, which I cannot judge from my own field and must leave to Eriksson, Mehlig and Danielsson.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict from my profile. I work in PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur, not in IceCube or atomic clocks, and have no stated ties to Katori, Ye or their institutions. In round 1 I noted a possible bias toward B043 from my own astroparticle detector background; since I no longer lead with it, that risk is smaller, but I keep the disclosure. As Chair I will bring the recusal questions raised by Kroll, Lindroth, Johansson and Olsson to the committee for a ruling and do not decide them alone.
